titulo: Today's loop engines: /goal, /loop, Ralph, routines, codex exec
lead: There are five common ways to put an agent in a loop, and they answer two questions differently: what triggers the next turn and who decides when to stop. Choosing wrong gets expensive: a /loop waiting for a condition that never comes, a /goal that believes what the agent said. Here is only what the official documentation confirms, read on 10/19/2026.
objetivo: choose the right loop engine for a task by knowing where it runs, what triggers the next turn, who decides when to stop, and the limit of each one.

aprende.t: /goal: by condition, with an evaluator that only reads the conversation
/loop and routines: by time or by event, and where each one runs
Ralph and codex exec: the disposable session inside a loop of your own

hero_alt: Stopwatch, stepper motor, mechanical timer, cloud-shaped part and server module lined up on a dark workbench.

secoes.sub: Click each engine: what triggers the next turn, who decides when to stop, and the limit the official docs give.

itens.t: Next turn: when the previous one ends
Stops: a small model judges the condition

nos.detalhe: After each turn, a small model judges your condition: met, not met, or impossible. It's a prompt-based Stop hook, per session. Limit: the evaluator doesn't run commands or read files, it only judges the conversation; the proof has to be printed out. It doesn't change the permission mode. With -p it runs to the end in a single call.

itens.t: Stops: you, or Claude decides it's done

nos.detalhe: Repeats a prompt at a fixed interval (/loop 5m …) or at one Claude picks on each round, from 1 minute to 1 hour. Limits: it belongs to the session and only fires while Claude Code is open and idle; minimum of 1 minute; a recurring task expires after 7 days; the self-paced one doesn't come back on --resume. It's for watching, not for chasing a condition.

itens.t: Next turn: the loop calls again

nos.detalhe: A technique described by Geoffrey Huntley: in its pure form, a bash loop that calls the agent with the same prompt, endlessly. Each session is disposable; what remains is in the files and in git. Anthropic cites the pattern as a community convergence. Limit: it has no stop or verification out of the box; you add those yourself (lessons 6 and 7).

itens.t: Trigger: schedule, HTTP call, or GitHub event
No access to your local files

nos.detalhe: A saved configuration (prompt, repositories, connectors) that runs on Anthropic's infrastructure, with your laptop closed. Limits: it's in research preview (behavior and limits may change); it works on a fresh clone, with no access to your local files; minimum interval of 1 hour on the schedule.

Runs Codex without an interface: it takes the request as an argument or via stdin, works, and exits. By default the sandbox is read-only; --sandbox workspace-write allows editing. --json gives the events as JSONL, -o saves the last message, exec resume --last continues the previous one. Limit: it isn't a loop; the loop, the test, and the stop live in a script of your own (the headless loop is course 2).

secoes.legenda: Sources: official Claude Code docs (/goal, scheduled tasks, routines) and Codex docs (non-interactive mode), read on 10/19/2026; ghuntley.com/ralph.

rolagem_fim.texto: Does the next turn come from a condition, a clock, or a loop of your own? And who decides to stop: an evaluator that reads the conversation, you, or a test that actually runs? The engine that runs the test outside the conversation is the hardest to fool.
rolagem_fim.curto: Condition, clock, or loop. Conversation or test.

secoes.sub: A rule of thumb based on the limits above.

passos.titulo: A task with a provable end
texto: Migrate a module until it compiles and the tests pass, empty a queue of issues. The condition needs an end state, the command that proves it, and what must not change along the way.
Put a cap on the condition itself, as the doc suggests: "or stop after 20 turns".

exemplo.texto: python3 -m pytest -q tests/ prints 6 passed, no file in tests/ was modified, or stop after 15 turns

passos.titulo: Watch something that changes on its own
texto: Did the deploy finish? Did the CI pass? Did a comment arrive on the PR? Time triggers the next round, and each round looks again.
Close the terminal and it stops. To last longer than the session, use a cloud schedule, the Desktop app, or GitHub Actions, as the doc itself points out.

passos.titulo: Hours of work on your machine
passos.sub: your own loop + codex exec or claude -p
texto: Each cycle is a new session that rereads the state from a file; what decides whether to continue is the test run by the script, not the conversation.
This is what the execucao-longa kit does, with a cap on time and memory (course 2).
PR review on an event, nightly issue triage: repeatable work in a repository, without depending on the files on your machine.
Since it is in research preview, check the limits in the doc before depending on it.

secoes.titulo: The five in one line each
secoes.sub: Commands from the official documentation and from the Ralph article. Run only the ones you will actually use.

blocos.conteudo:
/goal python3 -m pytest -q tests/ prints 6 passed and git diff --stat -- tests/ comes out empty, or stop after 15 turns
/goal clear

claude -p "/goal CHANGELOG.md has an entry for each PR this week" --output-format stream-json --verbose

/loop 5m check whether the deploy finished and tell me what happened
/loop check whether CI passed and reply to the review comments
while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done

codex exec "count the .md files in this folder and reply with just the number"
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write "create ola.txt with the word ola"
codex exec --json "summarize the repository structure" > eventos.jsonl
codex exec resume --last "now fix what you found"

abas.html: As written, the loop has no stop and no verification: it runs until you press Ctrl+C. The executable name in the article is the author's; on your machine it would be claude -p or codex exec -. In lessons 6 and 7 you add the done criterion and the caps that are missing.

The execucao-longa kit uses /goal in Codex as well (with /goals and /goal pause|resume). This track's research did not find the official page with its date and limits; so this course claims nothing beyond the use in the kit.

secoes.sub: On your machine. These are short runs: they use little of your quota.

exercicios.titulo: E1 · A /goal with proof in the output
exercicios.texto: In an empty folder with git initialized, open Claude Code and run: /goal the file ola.txt exists and cat ola.txt prints ola in the conversation, or stop after 5 turns.
exercicios.pronto: cat ola.txt → ola, and the goal status in Claude Code shows the condition as met, with the turn count.

exercicios.texto: In the same folder, ask Codex in headless mode to count files, writing the last message to a file.
exercicios.pronto: codex exec -o resposta.txt "how many .txt files are in this folder? answer with just the number"; echo "saída: $?" → saída: 0, and grep -cE '^[0-9]+$' resposta.txt → 1 (the answer is a single line with just a number; the criterion checks the format, not what the model answered).

exercicios.texto: List three real tasks of yours in a file motores.md, one per line, in the format task → engine → why (trigger and who decides to stop).
exercicios.pronto: grep -c '→.*→' motores.md → 3, and no task with a verifiable end was left with /loop.

perguntas.p: Your /goal condition is "all tests pass". The agent writes "I ran the tests, all pass" without showing the output. What happens?
opcoes: The evaluator runs the tests and checks
The evaluator only reads the conversation, so it may accept the agent's sentence
perguntas.explica: Per the doc, the evaluator does not run commands or read files: it judges what appeared in the conversation. That is why the condition asks for the proof to be printed ("npm test sai 0"). Course 1 shows how to make this shortcut-proof.

perguntas.p: You want to check the CI every 10 minutes during the afternoon, with the terminal open. Which engine?
perguntas.explica: It's time-based watching inside the session: the /loop case. /goal pursues a condition on every turn; routines is for when there is no open terminal.

perguntas.p: Why is a routine not suited to running the tests of a project that only exists on your laptop?
opcoes: Because it runs in the cloud on a fresh clone, with no access to local files
Because the minimum interval is 1 minute
Because it needs a paid API
perguntas.explica: The official table says: local file access, no (fresh clone). The routine's minimum interval is 1 hour; 1 minute is the one for /loop and Desktop.

perguntas.p: What is missing from Ralph in its pure form, while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude-code ; done?
opcoes: Stopping and verification: the loop has no end and no test
Action: it doesn't call the agent
perguntas.explica: The state lives in the files and in git, and each turn acts. But nothing decides that it's done and nothing checks the work: the two pieces you add.

perguntas.p: Will a recurring /loop created today still run a month from now?
opcoes: No: recurring tasks expire 7 days after they are created
Only if the session is resumed
perguntas.explica: The doc limits the lifetime of a forgotten loop: it fires one last time and deletes itself at 7 days. To last longer, recreate it or use a schedule outside the session.

itens.texto: Each engine differs in what triggers the next turn (condition, time, loop, event) and in who decides to stop.
/goal judges only the conversation; /loop lives in the session and expires in 7 days; routines run in the cloud without your files; codex exec is a single run, not a loop.
A loop that calls the agent with state in files; you add the stopping and verification.
